title: Interior and Radiators
premise: Lena Iversen, a night librarian in a city that never quite sleeps, has spent her adult life cataloguing silences — her own and her family's. When she finds a box of undelivered letters hidden behind her late grandmother's wardrobe, the letters reveal that her mother's disappearance thirty years ago was not abandonment but escape, arranged by the very relatives who raised Lena. As Lena tracks down the recipients who never received them, she discovers her mother may still be alive, and the family closes ranks to keep the arrangement buried. In the end, Lena must choose between preserving the inherited silence that kept her safe and delivering the truth at last — she mails the final letter, meets her mother once, and lets the family myth die so her own life can begin.
about_author: Cyrus Whitlock is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing unclaimed property in municipal storage, where he first encountered boxes of letters no one ever came for. He writes literary fiction about inheritance, secrecy, and the objects families leave behind.

chapters.title: The Night Shift of Small Hours
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Working nights at the Halvard Branch Library, Lena catalogs returned books and the small confessions readers leave in them. She describes her habit of writing down everything unsaid in a private ledger. Emotional beat: loneliness disguised as order; establish her compulsion to inventory what others avoid.

chapters.title: A House That Keeps Its Own Records
chapters.summary: POV Lena. After her grandmother Astrid's funeral, Lena returns to the old family house to sort it with her uncle Per, who controls every conversation by deciding what gets packed. Emotional beat: the choreography of avoidance; Per steers them away from the back bedroom without explanation.

chapters.title: Behind the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Alone in the house, Lena moves the wardrobe to check the radiator valve and finds a cavity containing a shoebox: forty-one letters, stamped, addressed, never sent — all in her mother Marit's handwriting, dated the year before she vanished. Emotional beat: vertigo; the inventory instinct fails her for the first time.

chapters.title: What the Letters Do Not Say
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Reading the first letters, Lena learns they were written to a woman named Signe in another city — warm, coded, increasingly desperate. None mention why they stopped. Emotional beat: hunger for a mother's voice colliding with the suspicion that the letters were intercepted.

chapters.title: Uncle Per's Version
chapters.summary: POV Per. Per narrates his own careful history: how he took in nine-year-old Lena, built a stable life, and buried his sister's 'selfishness.' He notices the wardrobe moved. Emotional beat: protective love curdled into control; he begins quietly checking on Lena's visits to the house.

chapters.title: The Address That Isn't Empty
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena travels to the address on the envelopes and finds an elderly neighbor who remembers Signe — and mentions, casually, that Signe had a visitor once, years ago, a man from this city. Emotional beat: the past proving porous; first crack in the official story.

chapters.title: Radiators and Other Things That Hum
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Back home, Lena fixes the failing radiator in her own apartment while rereading the letters, noticing references to 'the arrangement' and 'what we agreed.' Emotional beat: domestic warmth as metaphor — heat carried through hidden pipes, like secrets through a family.

chapters.title: Signe Answers the Door
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena locates Signe, now in her eighties, who recognizes the name Iversen before Lena says a word. Signe admits she wrote back — dozens of replies — and none arrived. Emotional beat: two custodians of the same silence meeting; grief and relief in equal measure.

chapters.title: Forty-One Letters, Forty-One Replies
chapters.summary: POV Signe (flashback frame). Signe recounts the correspondence: Marit planning to leave her marriage, asking Signe to help her disappear with her daughter. The last reply begged her to wait one more year. Emotional beat: the machinery of the plan revealed — and the moment it was sabotaged.

chapters.title: Who Collected the Mail
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Cross-referencing dates, Lena realizes someone in the house intercepted both directions of correspondence. Only three people had access: Astrid, Per, and her father Einar. Emotional beat: suspicion as a slow poison; Lena starts lying to Per about her whereabouts.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena reads her own accumulated notebooks and sees she has inherited the family method: recording instead of confronting. She writes her mother a letter she doesn't send. Emotional beat: self-recognition; the theme of inheritance turning inward.

chapters.title: Per Confronts the Wardrobe
chapters.summary: POV Per. Per searches the house, finds the box gone, and confronts his dead mother's memory — revealing to the reader that Astrid orchestrated the interception to keep Marit from taking Lena away. Emotional beat: Per's guilt reframed as devotion; he decides Lena must be protected from the truth, again.

chapters.title: Einar in the Care Home
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena visits her estranged father, diminished by early dementia, who mistakes her for Marit and says, 'You came back for the girl.' Emotional beat: devastating ambiguity — confession or confusion? Lena leaves shaking, certain only that he knew about the letters.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: POV Per. Per finally tells Lena his version: Marit wanted to flee with her, Astrid threatened to have her declared unfit, and the compromise was that Marit left alone and cut all contact — for Lena's sake, supposedly. Emotional beat: the family's founding bargain laid bare; Lena hears it as theft dressed as rescue.

chapters.title: Is She Alive?
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Signe reveals a detail she withheld: three years ago, a postcard arrived, unsigned, postmarked from a coastal town — proof Marit lived, or at least did then. Emotional beat: hope arriving late and dangerous; the clock starts ticking as Signe's health visibly fails.

chapters.title: Following the Postmark
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena takes leave from the library and travels to the coastal town, tracing the postcard through a boarding house register under a name from the letters. Emotional beat: the librarian learning to read a world without catalogues; fear and exhilaration braided together.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Feeds Gulls
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena finds her mother — older, watchful, feeding gulls on the pier — and cannot approach. She watches for two days, drafting and discarding openings. Emotional beat: paralysis at the threshold of the thing she wants most; the price of survival made visible in Marit's solitary life.

chapters.title: Per Follows
chapters.summary: POV Per. Having tracked Lena, Per arrives to stop the meeting, convinced it will destroy Lena as it destroyed Marit. He and Lena argue on the seafront while Marit watches them from a distance, unrecognized. Emotional beat: climax of the family pattern repeating itself in public; Per breaks down and admits he read every letter he stole.

chapters.title: Delivered at Last
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Lena walks the remaining letters to her mother's door and hands over the box — forty-one sentences finally delivered. Marit reads one aloud, then explains her side: she stayed away because Astrid made her believe contact would cost Lena everything. Emotional beat: catharsis without absolution; both women see the arrangement for what it was.

chapters.title: One Hour, No More
chapters.summary: POV Marit. Marit gives Lena a single hour, no promises beyond it. They talk plainly — about the father, the flight, the years. Marit asks nothing and offers nothing except the truth. Emotional beat: restrained devastation; love that cannot be converted into a life together, only acknowledged.

chapters.title: What Lena Keeps
chapters.summary: POV Lena. Returning to the city, Lena faces Per — not to forgive but to end the arrangement, telling him she will decide what she inherits. She keeps the letters, donates Astrid's furniture, and reopens the sealed back bedroom. Emotional beat: quiet severance; identity reclaimed from the family's architecture of silence.

chapters.title: Interior and Radiators
chapters.summary: POV Lena. A year later, Lena runs a night program at the library helping people write the letters they've postponed. She sends her mother a card each season; sometimes a reply comes. The radiators hum, the ledger holds fewer entries than before. Emotional beat: resolution — not reunion, but an honest warmth, maintained on purpose.
